source.title: Classification vs regression in overparameterized regimes: Does the loss function matter?
source.authors: Vidya K. Muthukumar; Adhyyan Narang; Vignesh Subramanian; Mikhail Belkin; Daniel J. Hsu; Anant Sahai

page_placements.theme: Margins and conventional complexity measures: risk prediction and failures

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper’s own feature-dimension sweeps report opposing test-error trends across linear feature ensembles, qualifying the generalization of risk-improves-past-interpolation claims.
record.gate_note: The paper cites double-descent work as background, but the catalog rows below use its own test-error results. Figure 4(b) also plots error against sample count for a bi-level ensemble; the text gives no directional result for that sweep, and its setting is not identified as near the interpolation threshold, so it is not recorded as a V3 result. The paper does not sweep training epochs or deep-network size.
record.test_reason: In Section 6 the paper runs its own sweeps of feature dimension d past interpolation (n = 32 fixed). It uses hard-margin SVMs on linear Gaussian feature models and reports the direction of test 0-1 loss. This is a new setting (classification with max-margin linear models) with a result on whether risk improves as capacity grows past interpolation (V4). The rest of the paper (SVM equals min-norm interpolation; classification-vs-regression regimes) does not sweep capacity through the interpolation threshold. T3 fits better than T5 because the paper does not argue that any double-descent version is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase over-weights Section 6. The main conclusions are: (1) with enough effective overparameterization, every training point is a support vector, so SVM, logistic and square-loss training give the same min-norm interpolator; (2) depending on effective overparameterization, that solution can succeed at both tasks, succeed at classification but fail at regression, or fail at both; (3) margin-based bounds are vacuous and uninformative here, since margin rises with d while test error rises (isotropic) or falls (weak features).
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes overparameterized linear models with Gaussian or weak-feature ensembles and compares test losses across feature dimensions; it does not reproduce the original deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature ensemble changes the direction of the test-error trend: error increases with feature dimension for isotropic Gaussian features and decreases for weak features.

fits_no_version.finding: With sufficient effective overparameterization, all training points become support vectors, so the hard-margin SVM equals min-norm interpolation (Thm 11, Fig 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In highly overparameterized linear models, max-margin and least-squares interpolating solutions coincide.

fits_no_version.finding: In the bi-level ensemble, a regime exists where min-norm interpolation has 0-1 test error tending to 0 but regression MSE tending to null risk (Thm 13, Fig 4a). Test loss rises with q (effective overparameterization) at fixed n and d.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign overfitting for classification needs milder conditions than for regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Margin-based generalization bounds exceed 1 (vacuous) and track neither the rising (isotropic) nor the falling (weak features) test error (Figs 5, 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalized margin does not predict generalization in overparameterized linear classifiers.

record.problems: The relevant feature-dimension evidence is shown in figures without extractable numerical values or reported uncertainty. The experiments hold n = 32 fixed and do not establish complete double-descent curves or test deep networks.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure 4(b) is not included because the text does not state the direction of the sample-count trend and the setting is not identified as near the interpolation threshold.

untested.parts: No deep networks; no model-size sweep through the interpolation threshold.
Figure 4(b) varies n with d = n^{3/2} in the bi-level ensemble, far from the interpolation threshold. There is no test of more data hurting near the threshold.

The under-parameterized U-shaped portion and the peak at interpolation are not shown. The d sweeps start only where all training points are support vectors. Only linear Gaussian / weak-feature models with an SVM are covered.
No single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
No label-noise or regularization sweeps affecting a peak. Label noise is stated not to change asymptotic scalings, but no peak is studied.
No re-plotting against an effective parameter count. The q parameter (effective overparameterization) at fixed d is a different axis.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Its bearing on double descent is limited to two figure-only d sweeps in the post-interpolation regime (Figs 5b, 6b). Neither shows a peak, so the evidence speaks only to the direction of risk past interpolation, which depends on feature distribution. I changed the tranche from T5 to T3. I treated the isotropic result as limits_scope rather than challenges: V4 is a general curve claim, and the paper presents isotropy as a known poorly generalizing case rather than a refutation.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-size double descent and its peak near the interpolation threshold.
Whether adding samples near the interpolation threshold raises test error.
The results are feature-dimension trends in two linear feature ensembles, not full curves across model classes; they do not establish the classical U-shaped portion or a peak near interpolation.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
Whether noise or regularization drives the peak, produces multiple peaks, or removes it under optimal tuning.
Whether re-counting complexity as effective parameters converts second descent to an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: Isotropic Gaussian features (Definition 4)
rows.size_stated: number of features d varied; n = 32
rows.operation_detail: Varied feature dimension d and measured test classification loss for the hard-margin SVM.
rows.value: figure only; text states that test classification loss increases as d increases
rows.note: The text says test classification loss increases with feature dimension, contrary to the risk-improves-past-interpolation direction. The figure does not provide extractable point values.
rows.check: State is fine: the text says test classification loss increases with d for isotropic features. Caveats: figure only, with no point values. The sweep covers only the 'sufficiently overparameterized' range where all points are support vectors, so it does not reach the interpolation threshold or any peak. The paper attributes the rise to isotropic features generalizing poorly (Theorem 13), with a 1-sparse signal.

rows.subject: Weak features ensemble (Definition 9)
rows.size_stated: number of features d varied; n = 32
rows.operation_detail: Varied feature dimension d and measured test classification loss for the hard-margin SVM.
rows.value: figure only; text states that test classification loss decreases as d increases
rows.note: This is a decreasing-error trend in the feature-dimension sweep; the paper does not report extractable point values or the full double-descent curve.
rows.check: State is fine as a direction: test loss decreases as d increases for weak features (sigma = 0.1). Caveats: figure only, with no values. The sweep is confined to the highly overparameterized regime, so the first descent and the peak are not shown. The paper notes weak features are 'known to exhibit the double-descent behavior.'

relationships.condition: Isotropic Gaussian features, 1-sparse signal, hard-margin SVM, n = 32, d well past interpolation
relationships.reason: Test 0-1 loss rises as d grows past interpolation (r1). In this feature distribution, extra capacity does not improve risk; the paper ties this to isotropy generalizing poorly (Thm 13).
relationships.display_finding: Test classification error increased as d grew beyond interpolation, with poor generalization attributed to isotropic features.

tranche.reason: Section 6.2 explicitly reports reversed post-interpolation improvement for isotropic features and improvement for weak features. These results require qualifying V4 by feature geometry, meeting the T5 definition.
